titleText.es: Oye, ¿qué probabilidad había de que hubiera cinco fans de Ayn Rand en el mismo tren? Deben de ir a una convención.
titleText.en: Hey, what are the odds -- five Ayn Rand fans on the same train! Must be going to a convention.
titleText.noteEn: The official English title blends sheep and people as Sheeple. The Spanish archive uses the broader livestock title Ganado while preserving the sheep comparison in ovejas.

regions.labelEs: MIRA ESTA GENTE. AUTÓMATAS DE MIRADA BOVINA SOMETIDOS A SU RUTINA DIARIA, SIN PARARSE NUNCA A MIRAR A SU ALREDEDOR Y PENSAR. SOY EL ÚNICO SER HUMANO CONSCIENTE EN UN MUNDO DE OVEJAS.

applications.explanationEn: Mira is the affirmative informal command used to tell one familiar person to look.
Sometidos comes after the expanded noun phrase headed by autómatas and describes that group.
Sometidos uses masculine plural -os to match the mixed or masculine plural group autómatas.
Bovina follows the noun mirada in the common neutral order for a descriptive adjective.
Bovina uses feminine singular -a to match the feminine singular noun mirada.
Sometidos matches the plural people, a introduces the controlling condition, and su rutina diaria fills that condition slot.
Diaria follows rutina in the common neutral order for a descriptive adjective.
Diaria uses feminine singular -a to match the feminine singular noun rutina.
Sin introduces an action that does not happen, and pararse remains in its unchanged dictionary form with se attached.
The pronoun se is attached to the end of the unchanged infinitive parar, producing the single written word pararse.
Pararse supplies the pause, a links it to the next action, and mirar stays in its unchanged dictionary form; nunca adds the visible ‘ever’ meaning inside the negative setting.
A and alrededor form the location expression, while su identifies the people whose surroundings are meant.
Humano follows the noun ser, and consciente follows that complete noun expression to add a second description of the same being.
Único and humano use masculine singular -o to match ser. Consciente is also singular; its ending works with either masculine or feminine nouns, while its plural would be conscientes.

applications.exampleEs: SOY EL ÚNICO SER HUMANO CONSCIENTE
applications.explanationEn: Soy is a form of ser because the following noun phrase presents the speaker's claimed identity rather than a physical location.

cards.promptEs: orden afirmativa para tú: habla, come, escribe
cards.questionEn: How do you give one friend or familiar person a positive command?
cards.answerEn: Use the informal singular command form, often the same form used for “he” or “she” in the present.
cards.noteEn: For many regular verbs, -ar becomes -a and -er or -ir becomes -e: hablar becomes habla, comer becomes come, and escribir becomes escribe. Some common verbs are irregular or change their stem. Negative commands use a different form and are a separate pattern.

example.es: Abre la ventana.
example.en: Open the window.

cards.promptEs: autómatas · único ser humano consciente · mundo de ovejas
cards.questionEn: What undercuts the speaker's claim to be the only independent thinker?
cards.answerEn: The same thought bubble belongs to all five train passengers: each person privately believes everyone else is an unthinking sheep while imagining themself uniquely conscious. Their supposedly individual insight is therefore identical and collective.
cards.noteEn: The official English title Sheeple blends sheep and people. The title text calls the passengers Ayn Rand fans; Rand is associated with philosophical individualism, which sharpens the irony of five people making the same self-exception.
An autómata is a machine or a person imagined as moving without independent thought. The plural autómatas can refer to a mixed or masculine group.

example.es: La novela presenta a los trabajadores como autómatas.
example.en: The novel presents the workers as automatons.

cards.questionEn: Where does a basic Spanish describing word usually go relative to its noun?
cards.answerEn: Put it after the noun in the common neutral order.
cards.noteEn: Many ordinary descriptive words follow the person or thing they describe: un coche rojo, una casa grande. Some adjectives commonly come before the noun, and moving an adjective can change emphasis or meaning, so this is a useful default rather than an absolute rule.

example.es: Necesito una mochila nueva.
example.en: I need a new backpack.

cards.promptEs: adjetivo que concuerda con masculino o femenino
cards.questionEn: How does a Spanish describing word change for a man, woman, or gendered noun?
cards.answerEn: Make the describing word match the gender and number of the person or thing it describes.
cards.noteEn: Many describing words ending in -o change to -a for a feminine singular person or noun: cansado becomes cansada. Plurals normally add -s. Some describing words have one form for both genders.

example.es: Pedro está cansado y Ana está cansada.
example.en: Pedro is tired and Ana is tired.

cards.noteEn: De plus a noun phrase can describe what kind of thing something is or a characteristic it has. English may use “with,” “having,” or a compound adjective.

example.es: Buscan una casa de gran tamaño.
example.en: They are looking for a large house.

cards.noteEn: Mirada can name the act or manner of looking, and it can also mean a way of viewing a topic.

example.es: El libro ofrece una mirada distinta al problema.
example.en: The book offers a different look at the problem.

cards.noteEn: Bovina describes a feminine singular noun and can literally mean related to cattle or figuratively suggest a dull, passive expression.

example.es: La figura tenía una expresión bovina.
example.en: The figure had a bovine expression.

cards.noteEn: Sometidos comes from someter. Its -os ending matches a masculine or mixed plural group.

example.es: Los planes están sometidos a revisión.
example.en: The plans are subject to review.

cards.questionEn: How do you say that someone or something is subject to a rule, force, or condition?
cards.answerEn: Use the matching form of sometido followed by a and the condition.
cards.noteEn: Choose sometido, sometida, sometidos, or sometidas to match the person or thing affected. The preposition a remains unchanged before what imposes the control or constraint.

example.es: La decisión está sometida a varias reglas.
example.en: The decision is subject to several rules.

cards.answerEn: to; required after sometido before what imposes the constraint
cards.noteEn: Sometido, sometida, sometidos, and sometidas normally use a before the rule, force, or condition that something is subject to.

example.es: El horario está sometido a cambios.
example.en: The schedule is subject to changes.

cards.noteEn: Su stays singular because the possessed thing is singular, even when the owners are several people. Sus is used before a plural possessed thing.

example.es: Los alumnos conocen su materia.
example.en: The students know their subject.

cards.noteEn: Diaria is the feminine singular form of diario because it describes a feminine singular noun.

example.es: Caminar forma parte de mi rutina diaria.
example.en: Walking is part of my daily routine.

cards.questionEn: How do you say that someone does one thing without doing another?
cards.answerEn: Put sin before the second action verb in its unchanged dictionary form.
cards.noteEn: The dictionary form is the unchanged verb ending in -ar, -er, or -ir. When the same person performs both actions, Spanish uses sin directly before that form; it does not add a word equivalent to English “-ing.”

example.es: Salió sin cerrar la puerta.
example.en: She left without closing the door.

cards.noteEn: Pararse uses the attached pronoun se. Before another action, pararse a means to stop what one is doing in order to perform that action.

example.es: Se paró a escuchar la música.
example.en: He stopped to listen to the music.

cards.promptEs: verbo en forma de diccionario + pronombre unido
cards.questionEn: Where can a short object word such as me, te, lo, or la go with an unchanged action verb?
cards.answerEn: Attach it to the end of the verb and write the result as one word.
cards.noteEn: An unchanged dictionary-form verb ends in -ar, -er, or -ir. Short object words can attach directly: conocer + te becomes conocerte, and ayudar + me becomes ayudarme.

example.es: Quiero ayudarte.
example.en: I want to help you.

cards.questionEn: How do you say that someone pauses in order to do an action?
cards.answerEn: Use the needed form of pararse, then a, then the action verb in its unchanged dictionary form.
cards.noteEn: The small pronoun changes with the person: me paro, te paras, se para, nos paramos, or se paran. A remains before the following action.

example.es: Nos paramos a leer el aviso.
example.en: We stopped to read the notice.

cards.answerEn: ever (after a negative idea such as sin)
cards.noteEn: Nunca often means ‘never.’ When sin has already supplied the negative meaning, natural English commonly uses ‘ever’: sin mirar nunca atrás means ‘without ever looking back.’

example.es: Salió sin mirar nunca atrás.
example.en: He left without ever looking back.

cards.answerEn: to; links pararse to the action someone stops to do
cards.noteEn: Use a between a form of pararse and the following action verb in its unchanged dictionary form.

example.es: Nos paramos a descansar.
example.en: We stopped to rest.

cards.answerEn: no separate English word; begins a su alrededor, ‘around them’
cards.noteEn: The location expression uses a before mi, tu, or su alrededor. Natural English translates the whole expression rather than a by itself.

example.es: Ella miró a su alrededor.
example.en: She looked around her.

cards.questionEn: How do you say ‘around me,’ ‘around you,’ ‘around us,’ or a similar idea?
cards.answerEn: Use a, then a possessive word such as mi, tu, su, nuestro, or vuestro, then alrededor.
cards.noteEn: The possessive word identifies whose surrounding area is meant. Su can refer to one or more people, so the situation tells whether it means around him, her, or them; nuestro means around us, and vuestro means around plural informal ‘you’ in Spain.

example.es: Miramos a nuestro alrededor antes de seguir.
example.en: We looked around us before continuing.

cards.noteEn: In a mi, tu, or su alrededor, alrededor refers to the surrounding area and natural English says ‘around me, you, him, her, or them.’

example.es: Mira a tu alrededor.
example.en: Look around you.

cards.promptEs: ser para identidad · estar para ubicación
cards.questionEn: Which Spanish “to be” verb says what something is, and which says where it is?
cards.answerEn: Use ser for identity or a defining description; use estar for the location of a person or thing.
cards.noteEn: This contrast is not simply permanent versus temporary. Forms of ser such as soy and es identify or describe what something is. Forms of estar such as están normally locate people and things. Events are a common exception: Spanish uses ser to say where or when an event takes place.

example.es: El museo es famoso y está en Madrid.
example.en: The museum is famous and is in Madrid.

cards.noteEn: Único changes to única, únicos, or únicas to match the person or thing it describes.

example.es: Es el único camino abierto.
example.en: It is the only open road.

cards.noteEn: Ser usually appears as the dictionary form “to be.” With an article, el ser can instead be a noun meaning a being, existence, or the self.

example.es: El ensayo reflexiona sobre el ser.
example.en: The essay reflects on being.

cards.noteEn: Consciente has the same singular form for masculine and feminine nouns; its plural is conscientes.

example.es: Soy consciente del problema.
example.en: I am aware of the problem.

cards.noteEn: Oveja is grammatically feminine. The plural ovejas can refer to multiple sheep regardless of their sex.

example.es: Las ovejas cruzaron el campo.
example.en: The sheep crossed the field.
